utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Buja, if I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I begin may I just raise quickly one administrative matter which is of some significance. There seems to be no rhyme or reason at the beginning of the sessions as to access to those defendants who wish to be seen. And today, for example, there was no access before we sat. I don't know the reason; I haven't been given any. But it is, we think and we would submit desirable for a short time. It's only ever 15 minutes, but there may be things to discuss. If Your Honour was in a position to indicate that desirability, then perhaps in the future there can be some pattern whereby we know we can have 15 or 20 minutes before we sit, because the 10 minutes or 20 in the intervals during the afternoon can also be used, but with witnesses like this it's really quite significance. I merely raise it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, this Chamber has never had to look into this issue, which suggests that it may not have been a feature in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My mind immediately registers the fact that the need to coordinate those leaving after the morning session and those coming in for the afternoon session may produce timing difficulties. I don't know. That was just my first impression. It would seem to me that it ought to be a matter that might be explored first by counsel with the registrar and the security people, and if there is no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Resolution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- satisfactory resolution, we would have to start the difficult process of trying to find out why and what might be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can leave it in your hands for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, good afternoon. Have you had an opportunity overnight to reread the Albanian version of the statement you made in October 2001 for the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read anything because I didn't get any document. I tried to recollect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry that you didn't have the document to take away. I'd hoped you would, but in any event we can do it now. Could you please have the Albanian version of this statement, which if you -- page numbers are required it's 03090415 is where it begins. Is there a copy in front of you now? There was last night. Do you have it in front of you now, the Albanian version?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just to get your bearings you'll see on the first sheet which I referred to yesterday is your name and the dates on which you were interviewed and the interviewee -- interviewer's name, Mr. Barney Kelly. So I now turn to the next page which -- in which there are introductory matters. It's your page -- I'm going to use the numbers at the top right-hand corner for you, if you can follow them. The last four digits of the page you have is 0416. Is that all right? You're following that? And 0417 in your copy is equivalent to our 9545 in which you're dealing with the killing of Adem Jashari and other matters, which I don't go into at this stage on that page. I want to now turn particularly to your arrival in Drenica which you have on page 0418 and we have at the top of page 9546. Now, on your page, it's the paragraph that begins with the words "when we arrived in Drenica valley." Do you have that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph down on page 0418.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, what I'm going to do because it's quicker this way if you wouldn't mind following it in the Albanian, I'm going to read it in English, this paragraph, and then the one below it and stop and ask you some questions. So I'm going to read it as we have it in English; please follow it. "When we arrived in Drenica valley from Vlan in March 1998, five of our units separated, namely Agim Bajrami; Ismet Jashari; Haxhi Shala, nicknamed Topi; myself; and Fatmir Limaj, 34 years, nicknamed Celiku, from Banje the municipality of Malisevo. He was in charge of this unit. We separated by order of the KLA main HQ to go and recruit for the war in other areas. We had to organise units in Shtime, Malisevo, Rance, in Shtime municipality Ferizaj, the biggest towns in the area. We had a designated territory to deal with the military structure which was later referred to as the Pastrik and the Nerodime zones. They were separate and operated according to their AORs, areas of responsibility. Fatmir Limaj became commander of one of Pastrik's four brigades, the 121 Brigade, which was founded during the first offensive by the Serbs in July 1998. It covered Malisheve and Lipjan. The brigade had their HQ in the village of Klecka, in Lipjan. He went into the KLA main HQ in November 1998 and remained a member there." And then the next paragraph, still on your same page: "Hashim Thaqi ordered the recruitment campaign. He received it from the KLA general commander whom we did not know at that time. Later on I came in contact with the general commander because I was a zone commander. Hashim Thaqi was never the commander of the KLA. Azem Syla, aged 45 years from Kishna in Gllogovc municipality, was the then-general commander of the KLA and was at the Rambouillet conference in February 1999." Now, is it right to say that in these paragraphs - and in the rest of the statement, for that matter, but particularly these paragraphs - you do not suggest that there was before the zones were set up, the subzones were established in 1998, any intermediate level of command between the General Staff and the units that you had to go and set up; and that the reason it's not mentioned is there was no intermediate level of command at that stage in Celiku with -- in Klecka with Commander Celiku, was there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though it's rather long, what you put to me, and trying to shed light on these issues. I think I've been very clear here about the fact that the units we were tasked to set up. I was myself settled in Shtime municipality and I explain here also about Agim Bajrami whose responsibility was to set up the unit in Kacanik, whereas Fatmir Limaj had the responsibility to set up in the unit in Malisheve. The form of command was based on guerrilla units. And the orders to these units were given by the General Staff. I'm saying here in full responsibility that if Fatmir Limaj was my commander, I would have pointed that out. And more than that, I would feel proud to do that because I have an extraordinary respect for this young man who did so much for our national -- for our liberation war. I would have felt proud, as I said, to do that. But this was not the case. In my public statements I have all -- often mentioned the fact that Fatmir Limaj have escorted me and I have referred to him as my first commander as a sign of respect even though the structure then was not so; that is, he was not my commander. And I was higher in rank in the period when I was appointed commander of the subzone of the Nerodime operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to pass to the question of zones, if you wouldn't mind. Is this right -- you do mention it. I don't ask you to look at it for the moment. It's in this statement you made -- historically it appears that the position was this: That certain areas in the early 1990s were given zones by the KLA and they were country areas, for example, Macedonia, Serbia, Kosovo, and Montenegro, but that strategy of giving zones to countries was later changed. Now, first of all, that's the first point I want to make. In other words, Kosovo had a zone number of its own, and that's why we started talking about subzones. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I will explain this issue. Initially the idea and the purpose of the KLA was to wage the war to liberate the territories occupied. Initially this was done through zones, zone number 1 was Kosova where the operation was taking place, the action was taking place. In zone number 2, which we called the territory under Macedonia, we didn't operate but the idea was to liberate the occupied territories of Albania. Zone number 1 was divided afterwards in subzones, and after the first contacts with the international politicians by the General Staff and their insistence for us not to spread out the conflict which might be fraught with tragic consequences for the entire Balkans. The policy of the KLA changed and it was focused only in Kosova, in zone number 1, as we used to refer to it then. And the action of the KLA at a later phase, especially in November and December, was on decision of the General Staff as subzone. So the zones were divided into subzones because the entire territory of Kosova was thought to be the entire territory where the KLA operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, if we look at in your page of the Albanian statement page 0419; in ours 9546, same page you were looking -- well, same page we were looking at but next page for you. You will see there you indicated the seven subzones and their areas of responsibility. I'm not going to read them all out, but there they are set out in your statement, are they not, the seven subzones? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have mentioned the subzones here and the area where they extended. Initially the subzones were organised on the basis of the municipalities. If you want me to describe the zones the way they were organised, I can do that, even though I don't know all the zones, meaning what municipalities they comprised. But I know more my zone which covered part of Lipjan, the Shtime municipality, Ferizaj, Kacanik, and later Terpeze municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I only really want to concentrate on three of the subzones as you have them in the statement, Drenica number 1, Pastrik number 2, and Nerodime number 6. You've indicated they were based on municipalities and I wonder, if you wouldn't mind, to ask you this: Firstly, when do you believe it was that you were appointed as the subcommander for Nerodime?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the commander of Nerodime subzone I was appointed on the 6th of July even though I have often thought it to be the 6th of June. But after looking at the decision I realised it was the 6th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, that's why I asked you about that. Now, in relation to that subzone in July -- beginning of July, I want to ask you specifically whether the following villages came within the Nerodime zone or whether they came within the Pastrik zone, do you follow, the particular villages and areas. First of all, Kroimire. Which subzone was that in?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July it was in the subzone of Nerodime because it was a village of Lipjan municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Right. Petrastica?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petrastica, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Fustica?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fustica, at least this is what I believed, was part of Lipjan municipality and it came within the subzone that I was supposed to organise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The reason I want to ask you this carefully is because of obviously what is said later. I'd like you to take this plan, if you wouldn't mind. We will have it in another form. It's map number 6 in P1 and this is a copy of it. I wonder if you would take the plan, please. And if it could be put on the monitor and then if you could mark -- what I'm going to ask you to do kindly once you've had a look at it and got your bearings -- I just explain what I'd like you to do and then if you'd just look at the map and see if you can do it. I'd like you to mark, so far as you are able to, the border between the two zones, the two subzones that we're talking about, Pastrik and Nerodime, because you can see on this plan that the three -- three of the villages I've just mentioned that you've just said were in the zone are all marked on this plan. And if you would very kindly, therefore, mark a line down the plan and where you thought your -- the zone you were commander of finished and where Pastrik zone began. Are you able to do that? And if you have a -- first of all, can you do that or not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best, although at that time the organisation was -- of subzones was done on the basis of municipalities without drawing any very clear-cut dividing line of inclusion of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. You indicated yesterday, maybe and the day before, the zones in fact -- there were villages on one side of the Berisa Mountains and villages on the other side of the Berisa Mountains was one way of looking at it. So if you can mark - however difficult it is and it's too difficult don't do it - would you mark with a pen if you have one on the map that you have in front of you where you thought the border ran, roughly speaking, between those two zones.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kroimire village, Pjetershtice, Shale, Bajice, Resinovc, up to Fushtice, lower Fushtice, and then it was linked with the other part of Lipjan where we didn't have units then. Nekovce we thought should be part of it, including the villages of Shtime and Ferizaj. There wasn't any clear-cut line, as I said, but it was based on municipalities. This part. Then comes the Lipjan municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could -- Your Honour, I wonder if that could become an exhibit. I don't know which one we're up, 160 something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P161 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: D not P. And L. We'll get a number in a little while, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The system is not giving the court officer what's needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If I can just return to your statement. In relation to these two zones, that's Pastrik and Nerodime, on the same page that you have and on the same page that we were looking at, you indicated in the Milosevic statement who the commanders and deputy commanders were of those various subzones, in particular 1, 2, and 6. I don't ask you to read them out; you've written them out in that statement and it's very clear. Do you see that in your statement, your page 0419; our page 9547 in this case?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what I want to suggest to you was abundantly clear at this time was once again Fatmir Limaj based in Klecka was not in command of any part of this zone, was he?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Fatmir Limaj was not appointed commander of any subzones at that time. At the end of the offensive, that is June/July, he had a brigade, he was a commander of a brigade in the Pastrik zone. I have explained here that the commander of Pastrik zone at that time was Musa Jashari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And if Celiku as you knew him, or Fatmir Limaj, had ever been a commander above you at this time of the subzones, would it be fair to say you would have expected him if he'd been above you throughout the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. previous period to himself have been appointed a subzone commander or been made a part of the General Staff? Is that a fair observation?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair observation, because Fatmir Limaj, if he had a higher rank, of course he would have been appointed the commander of a subzone or he would have become a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, just before we leave your statement in relation to subzones and so forth, are you in a position to confirm that Lapusnik was in the subzone of Drenica?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm it officially, but I do know that when we were appointed commanders of subzones, this was done on the basis of the villages of the municipalities. And to my recollection, Lapusnik and Negrovce, Kizhareke villages were part of the former Gllogovc commune, as it was called, in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to move from that statement and also the map. I want to move on to a much later period, in other words the period when you come here to give evidence. And you have recognised that there was when you got here what's called a proofing session. Do you recall the proofing session? Sorry, the question is: Do you recall that proofing session before you gave evidence when you came here to The Hague when you spoke to the Prosecution? It's a word you've used, sir. When you spoke to Mr. Whiting, I believe.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. You mean here, when I came in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's when you came here. I'm just using a word you used - I thought you understood it - if you don't I'll explain. When you arrived here in The Hague on this occasion to give evidence in this matter, there was a time when you met Mr. Whiting - he's the gentleman to your right who asked you questions and has been asking you questions for about a week - you met him and you discussed some part of your evidence or what you were going to say. Do you remember that occasion here in The Hague, this month probably?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that's what I want to ask you about. You've already indicated that you told Mr. Whiting a number of things. What we understand you told him was firstly, that the structure of the KLA that you had described in your interview in April 2003, the structure of the KLA between May and July, was wrong; that's the first thing. Second thing, that Fatmir Limaj was not your commander after you had entered Kosovo in March 1998. Now, firstly is that what you told Mr. Whiting in this proofing session?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this proofing session or preparatory meeting, as they say, I met with Mr. Whiting and we talked about issues about which -- about which he asked me. I didn't have the text of the statement -- of my statement even then. So I spoke about what I thought were wrong in my statement, and I clearly stated that whatever I had said about Fatmir Limaj, he was not my commander. He is never -- he was never my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Whiting keep notes that you could see or someone else of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Present at that meeting was also the investigator, Ole Lehtinen, and he kept notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate previous matters relating to this issue but I would once again ask that we have the notes of this particular meeting, given its significance. But may I just pass on for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What questions or what issues were raised by Mr. Whiting or the investigator that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this session -- in fact, there were two sessions; they were brief. In the first session I was asked about the structure, and we mentioned also the detentions or the stops that I have spoken about. In the second session they showed me some photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: When you -- I just want to concentrate at the moment on the issue of structure and Fatmir Limaj not being your commander. When you told them that, did either of them say to you, Oh, look here, that's not what you told us before; we better go through this interview and sort out what you meant? Did either of them say that to you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not exactly in this way, but they were calm when I mentioned that, namely that Fatmir Limaj has been -- never been my commander as well as when I spoke about those -- the process of stopping people, mentioning the case of my brother and other instances. And then I wanted to dwell on this issue of stopping people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did anyone in the room during this meeting suggest to you that if you said these things, the Prosecution may have to essentially suggest that you're lying?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember to have been told this in this form as you are putting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Please understand, I don't know what happened; we don't have the notes. I merely want to find out what happened. Roughly how long just in terms of -- was it half an hour each of these sessions or 20 minutes or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have lasted about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: During this time, did either Mr. Whiting or the investigator go back over any parts of your interview of 2003, pointing out what you had said then?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked, even though I didn't remember the questions put to me during the interview in 2003. So I tried to explain even then that I never had the text of the statement, which I couldn't confirm as my own and appear here before the Trial Chamber and swear and speak under oath about things when I hadn't seen the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I just clarify one thing. Is it right that you were never provided with a -- I can call it a hard copy or a type-up version in Albanian of the April 2003 interview. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, the question I now have is this: When did you first become aware that what you may have said or did say in your interview in 2003 was incorrect in relation to Fatmir Limaj and the structure of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my suspicions even earlier, because during the time that the interview was taken, on the suggestions that Barney Kelly made to me I gave the interview hoping that the same procedure followed during the trial against Milosevic would be followed, and that I would have occasion to review it, recollect events, and improve mistakes that I may have made, and then sign such a statement. This didn't happen and I started to suspect that this statement might be misused, especially so after the meeting with Ole Lehtinen, whom I asked to provide me with the text of the statement, which he didn't. I also explained to him that some of the witnesses who had been interviewed had their statements given to them and that it was only when I came here that I was provided with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to leave that topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just before I got to another topic all to go to, if it saves time, if the notes are available may we have them during the first break later this afternoon so we don't have to ask for this witness to come back. We do suggest clearly in what we's saying this has a bearing on a number of factors certainly which we would want to submit upon and that Your Honours may want to see. So unless there's objection I would like copies, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to the procedures that have been followed in this trial and approved as I understood it by the Trial Chamber in its decision on proofing, the Prosecution disclosed by a memorandum to the Defence new information that was disclosed during the proofing. That has been done. That has been referred to. I don't see any further basis or necessity for disclosure of notes. I don't see why that's required. I don't also frankly see why it's particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything further, Mr. Mansfield, you wish to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, there is, but I won't take up time. May I do it later, certainly not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, then we will move on. But before you do, we will have the exhibit number we've been waiting for.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be DL2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: DL2, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to move with your help -- before we get to the actual interview itself, there's one other matter I want to ask you about and that is your second arrest. You told us about a first arrest yesterday. A second arrest that took place in 2004. And my first question is: What was the allegation against you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was arrested in March last year, if I remember right, and my arrest was rather harsh. I was arrested -- they threw a sack over my head and my family didn't know my whereabouts for some days. I was sent to various places and I didn't know where I was -- or where I was being sent. And after 48 hours with my hands tied, I even slept with my hands tied, then after that they untied my hands after the doctors intervened. And this conduct towards me was mentioned even in a report of the department of state on the protection of human rights published recently. This conduct, this behaviour, which I -- towards me, which I never understood why, never understood why I was imprisoned about the March events when I was invited by the security troops to help me because of my authority I enjoyed in Ferizaj and Lipjan municipalities. I helped them. I called on the youths not to escalate into violence and I failed to understand why I was arrested. I had the impression after some days, after I was questioned several times in relation to those events, I was obliged to tell them precisely where I was, at what place, at what time. Then after 15 days a representative of the Prosecution -- Prosecutor's office, together with an interpreter, came to visit me. They showed me a letter. They translated the letter to me. The letter was addressed to the KFOR commander. The letter, if I could paraphrase it, that I was a man who speaks the truth, and the Prosecutor's office doesn't have to do with any violation on my part in Kosova and that the KFOR should know that I was a witness in the case against Milosevic and that I was also a witness to the crimes perpetrated by the Albanians. To this I reacted because I had never said anything. I never even thought that Albanians had committed any crimes. And then I suggested to the representative of the Prosecutor's office that with this I did not reconcile and that I would revise my stance -- my position after my release. My release occurred after two or three days after this visit, and this created me the impression that the Prosecutor's office wanted to pressure me. And this is how I understood my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Two questions arising out of it. The original one was: What did you understand the allegation against you was that led to your detention on that occasion? What did you understand the allegation was? What was it you'd done wrong according to what you believed you were being told?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply didn't know I had made any mistake. The allegation made against me was -- consisted of a single line. It said: "Violation of Resolution 1244" and it was written by the KFOR commander. My release was done on the basis of a paper, a document, which said he is freed -- he is acquitted of the charges. And I think I was released after 17 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The second question arising out of this is: Can you help us as to who from the Prosecutor's office visited you whilst you were detained on this matter?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name of the person who came to see me on behalf of the Prosecutor's office. I know that he gave me a card, which I have at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So you still have the card at home, do you? So you would be able to let us know the name of the Prosecutor who came to see you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took his card. I think I have it at home. I'm not very sure, but I know that he represented himself to me as the representative of -- or he introduced himself to me as a representative of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did he say he knew -- why he -- how he knew that you were in detention?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. We didn't talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did he say why he'd come to see you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had come to give to me the letter of the Prosecutor's office sent to KFOR commander, to become -- to make me acquainted with that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Had you ever requested to see anyone from the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period during my detention, no, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I meant -- I'm sorry, my fault. I did mean in the period of detention. In the period of detention had you asked that any letter be sent on your behalf so that your release might be obtained?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I now want to turn to a further topic which is the question of the interviews themselves that had taken place in 2003 with the Office of the Prosecutor. Can I ask you if you still have the Albanian version of this interview, 28th of April, 2003, available to you there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not of the copy of 2003 interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buja, so you understand what I'm going to do with your help is to identify what I suggest are major serious and obvious errors in this interview, errors and mistakes that you made which I think to some extent you now accept. You made major mistakes in this interview, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did there come a time in the interview when you got a little more worried than the pressures you've already described about living in Kosovo and so on when the Prosecutor told you that your name had come up during their investigations? Do you remember that phrase being used?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, such phrases were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And how did you feel when that was being put to you during this or these interviews in April?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only during these interviews but it was quite a long period of pressures of this nature. I wouldn't say that these were from the Prosecution, but there were pressures since the times when I was commander of the sixth zone of the TMK when different delegations of the Red Cross came and other organisations, when they would bring lists with names and they told me that I was to be familiar with those issues. And when I would tell them that I was not familiar with them, I always tried to explain to them that my weapon never made a difference between an Albanian or a Serb. My weapon fired only at those who were coming in the direction of my positions. In these cases I was asked about names and about the whereabouts of these persons on the lists who were missing. At that time, it didn't make sense to me because we had more than 3.500 missing Albanians and these lists coming from the Serb occupier didn't make sense to me. But even then one of the reasons -- this was one of the reasons of my withdrawal from the TMK because I did not reconcile with the way of the organisation of the TMK and with the exclusion of certain members from the ranks of the TMK. And shortly after, I left the TMK. Later on, these contacts continued. I was summoned to clarify these issues and explain these issues, and questions that could have appeared during this interview were in that sense that they did not make me feel comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, may I go back to the interview in April 2003 and what I'm going to do -- there are four examples. Two of them mean replaying the clips, with Their Honours' permission, and then I have some questions on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. them. They have clip numbers, but so you can follow in the Albanian translation that you have the first one I'm going to ask you about is known as clip 6. In the English version it's at page 40 and in the Albanian version it's at page 43. Page 43 of the Albanian, page 40 of the English. And those who want to follow it on the original translation, as 8580. So I wonder if clip 6 could be shown again when you found the place in the transcript. Would you just follow it? You've seen it once yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm much obliged to the Prosecution for lining these clips up and one more. Clip 6, it's known as.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: "O.L.: Do you remember names of persons who were in charge of these points? "S.B.: Well, I can -- well, it -- I used to know them by -- mostly by their nicknames. "O.L.: Okay, yeah. Nickname is okay. "S.B.: Voglushi for Lapusnik. Voglushi or Qerqiz, one of them was for Lapusnik. Voglushi would come -- would often visit Kroimire. So he would come and bring along back-up units to help us during the offensive. The soldiers from Lapusnik were stationed here in Fushtice. So it was a sort of competition who would set up more points among the commanders. It was problematic in a way because you had to move soldiers from one point to another point in order to set up -- so there was a sort of overlapping responsibilities, interference with each other. So it's not -- it's my responsibility, no these are my soldiers, these are your soldiers. Yeah, I can't remember the name of the person in charge there because of this fact. There's been -- there's been many changes here, meaning this point. Kroimire would serve as a gathering point for soldiers. There was no such a thing as a stationed unit in that place. I and Luan used to stay here, so I and Luan stayed here often. Kumanova -- Kumanova used to stay in Klecka. So Kumanova was thought at least at that time by us as the highest-ranking person in Klecka and Celiku was considered or was thought to be by us some higher-up than Kumanova. "THE INTERPRETER: Can I ask again who was the highest-ranking person in Klecka? "O.L.: Yes. "S.B.: According to what we thought, Kumanova was the highest-ranking person in Klecka. Later Kumanova moved with units here and was stationed in Luzhnice and also the other point and on the other side of the asphalt road in Grejcec. So anybody who tried to expand and -- to expand and increase the number of these points. "O.L.: Okay. Do you want to do the clarification on that? "A.W.: The way I understand what you're saying is that Kumanova is -- has responsibility for Klecka, but then Celiku is above him in the structure. That's at least what I understood you to say. Is that right? "S.B.: So we thought Celiku was above this structure. "A.W.: But he was also in Klecka? "S.B.: Yes, he was in Klecka. Yeah, it was at that time, end of July, July 1998, that there -- there happened to be that other members who were thought to be members of the General Staff used to stay in Klecka. Or at least we thought they were from General Staff, but from main headquarters. "A.W.: Also in May, June, and July, all during those months Celiku was in Klecka? "S.B.: Yes, yes, he was there. "O.L.: And I'm still trying to clarify a little bit the role of Kumanova now, him being -- you're saying the highest ranking in Klecka. Did that mean that he was giving orders to these other points or was he just the leader of the soldiers in Klecka? "S.B.: I can't say because my contacts, my meetings were with Celik. But Kumanova would be -- would happen to be present there as well during my meetings with Celiku. So it was more -- it was more work based on consultations rather than orders. So let's say I was -- I was consulted or I was consulting or I was discussing about the weapons supply. "THE INTERPRETER: I'm sorry, there was a mistake. "S.B.: Weapons supply. Yeah, that's correct. So it was -- there were sort of deliberations, so it's better not to do or do that. If Celiku was not able to give a definite answer to questions that would arise then, then he would turn to the general -- to the main headquarters to get clear instructions. "A.C.: Can you just draw in above Klecka the linkage to the main headquarters of the KLA. Just to complete the diagram. "S.B.: No, well it's -- yeah, I'll put momentarily as a main headquarters. Also I can't say it's the other thing but let's leave it that way for a moment. "O.L.: Just to" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buja, I'm sorry, I've played it again to you in some detail because I want to be clear with you that what -- in these passages you have been taking a lot of nonsense, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many things were not clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Do you agree that the "many things" are serious mistakes on anybody's view? Serious mistakes you have made in this passage about Celiku, about Klecka, about Kumanova? Serious mistakes, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, structural mistakes because at that time it was a different structure. I attempted to clarify it on several occasions that we had no other relation with Celik except for advice and consulting. I mentioned here that I need to clarify things and here it is said that I have given clarifications. As for the structure, this is where things were entangled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, the first thing is that Kumanova wasn't the commander of Klecka, was he?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen Kumanova in Klecka and I made the descriptions that were not official. I didn't know who was who, I just mentioned who I seen there. Later I learned that Kumanova was not commander of Klecka but of Luznica, of the Luznica unit that also comprised part of Guzcevce [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: When you were saying - whether you meant it or why you were saying it is another matter - but when you were saying that he was the highest commander in Klecka and that Celiku was above him, that was all nonsense, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a huge mistake because I spoke on basis of impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And if you kindly have alongside you at the moment P159, please. It's page 00033675. 00033675. It's the diagram. Do you have the diagram in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, there came a moment where the tape excerpt ended a moment ago in which Mr. Cayley, Andrew Cayley, said: "Can you just draw in above Klecka the linkage of the main headquarters." And what you said according to the translation then was, in order to complete the diagram: "No -- well, it's -- yeah. I'll put momentarily as a main headquarters. Also, I can't say it was the other thing, but let's leave it that way for the moment." Now, that, I appreciate, is how it's actually translated at the time. And even on the later translation I suggest that what you were doing there, do you agree, was just following a suggestion that you should do that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On basis what I've seen during the interview, it appears that I followed that suggestion although I have mentioned even at that time that explanations are necessary regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And the reason I suggest it was a nonsense to ask you to do it let alone for you to actually do that is if you look at the diagram the time frame that Mr. Whiting was putting to you in this interview was May, June, and July. There was no way once the subzones were created that your subzone of Kroimire, Petrastica, Fustica, which are all on this diagram, none of them came under Klecka at that time, and I suggest not before, either. But in any event, after June/July, Kroimire, Petrastica and Fustica didn't come under Klecka at all, did they?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in the last couple of days I've tried to explain this issue that the period May, June, July was quite a rapid period, full of events, and therefore the description of structure could be false. For example, in May we can speak of a different form of structure; in part of June of quite another form of structure; and in July of a totally different structure because it's then when the subzones were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Why did you allow yourself to be led by those interviewing you to draw this diagram, given that fluid situation?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first interview I thought that regardless of the mistakes that might occur, I will give -- be given the opportunity to review this interview, to make the corrections, and to recollect the events, which was very difficult for me. Simply, I thought that a procedure that had been followed in the past would be followed again. I thought that I would be given the opportunity to describe events with greater precision than it is here in the interview. This is what made me not to think well during -- about this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm going to pass now to another passage --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And Your Honour it's a short one, and it hasn't been shown to far and it may be convenient to lead up to the break with it. With the help of the Prosecution -- I'm very grateful -- it's a clip, short clip, which appears on our page 51 in the English version and on the Albanian, I hope I've got it right, it's page 57. Albanian 57, English 51. And it starts on the English version a third of the way down the page when this witness is being asked when he was appointed to the subzone. So page 51 and page 57. If Mr. Buja would be kind enough to follow it on the Albanian. Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: "A.W.: Was it at the beginning -- was it in June that you got that appointment? "S.B.: Yes, in June. "A.W.: Okay, that's fine. "O.L.: And during this fighting in June and July, would you say that you stayed under the commander of Celiku? "S.B.: No. No, I was not under his authority, under his command. In June I was under the authority of the main headquarters. Because it later -- it later began gradually to take shape this command, this command -- "O.L.: Let's stick in June/July now 1998. "S.B.: As I said, yeah. In this period, June/July, things started to get clearer, began to take -- this is main headquarters. Jakup Krasniqi was known to be a member of the General Staff or main headquarters. And there were subzones then, operational subzones. At that time I didn't know how many subzones, but the subzone I was appointed to be a commander was operational subzone for Nerodime. I was -- so I was -- I was appointed as a subzone commander to set up the headquarters and organise the war there. This -- so that was -- approximately there was an idea about the structure, about the command now in June and July."

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The question on that clip is: That in fact that's an example, is it not, of where you have accurately described what the position was once the subzones had been created, June and July; that you weren't under the command of Celiku, you were under the command of the General Staff. And the Nerodime zone at that time, you've already described the villages that came within that zone, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad that this can be seen here. I have described June when I met with the member of General Staff Mr. Jakup Krasniqi and the beginning of the organisation of subzones. It is true that this began in June. Several subzone commanders were appointed in June. I don't know the exact dates when. I was appointed in July, myself. I started to work with a subzone before my appointment because following the suggestions from Jakup Krasniqi I was supposed to start with a structuring of the subzone according to the municipalities that were to comprise Nerodime subzone, operational subzone. So this was to comprise Shtime, Ferizaj, and part of Lipjan, while the dilemma was for Kacanik and Elez Han.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And the final question on this part is: Can you help us as to when you started work, having spoken to Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started to work in this regard in mid-June in order to organise better the existing units at that time, the Blinaje, Zborce, Carraleve, and Fushtice units. I have mentioned it here and I will repeat it, that as for Zborce and Carraleve, I had a limited scope of work because of the problems I faced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient moment? And I've got one more clip to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: A final clip to be played. You've seen it once before. It's very short indeed. It's clip number 12 and you will find the Albanian -- Albanian translation is on page 64 of yours. We have it on page 55. So if that could just be played. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: "O.L.: So once again I want to go back to the period of June and July of 1998 and the area that was under the headquarters of Klecke. So was this organisation that you -- that you've drawn to us on this piece of paper, was this effective during this time period that you're calling the first offensive? "S.B.: Yeah, there were points at that time existent. "O.L.: Okay. And this was approximately the organisation in -- under the headquarters of Klecka?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If you still have your page open, Mr. Buja, you will see that in fact having been put to you that it was approximately the organisation of the authority under Klecka. On the transcript that you have you agree that's right with the question again. The simple point I want to put to you once again is that this was nonsense in June and July. That was not -- the diagram was not the organisation then and Nerodime wasn't under the headquarters of Klecka, was it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already explained these issues, namely that in June/July of 1998 the structure -- the commanding structure began to be clarified. Klecka as a place name, as a toponym that I have used, I had in mind the spokesperson of the KLA. And this was a person I had in mind, the spokesperson who had come up publicly, because that was the person with whom I consulted. And through him I got the orders and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but the particular villages, we've been through it before, that you put on the diagram, particular villages in fact came within Nerodime, that's Kroimire, Petrastica, and Fustica were all coming within the subzone of Nerodime, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I already explained. It was the period of when the idea of the organisation of subzones was launched and instructions were issued to me regarding the organisation of the units in the Lipjan municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And finally on this your chain of command was as subzone commander directly to a representative of the General Staff at that time you understood to be Krasniqi. Is that right, Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now I want to pass to another topic. I'm not going to play you this section; you had it played yesterday. The points I want to make are better on the transcripts themselves. In the English version of the transcript it's our page 76, and on yours, that is the Albanian version, it's page 92. And I'm to go slowly here because I want to make sure I've identified the right passage. Now, in the English version, bear with me, please, I want to start, and this is concerning the topic of the tractor, all right, that's what we're on about here and speaking with Celiku about the topic of the tractor. Now, in our version I want to start with the question: "Did you speak on any occasion with Celiku?" And that comes at the top of your page 92 I think.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said yesterday with Celiku I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, can I just intervene. I'll allow you plenty of time to explain if you wish to. I just want you to identify so you've got the right place in your statement, so I'll just go through it. You will remember this passage played yesterday. First of all, once again, there are major mistakes about this, are there not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see how it's been said in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: First of all, if there was an incident with a tractor and some people on the back of it or in it, it certainly didn't happen in Kroimire around the 25th and 26th, because you weren't there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. On the 25th, 26th, and 27th of July, because of the problems I had with the military structure there, I didn't set foot on Kroimire on those dates. I know that on the 23rd and 24th I've been in Kroimire and Fushtice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Secondly in this section where you'll telling the investigators about an incident with a tractor and a conversation with Celiku - you can read through it if you wish. I'm not going to take up Tribunal time - the word "prison" or reference to Lapusnik as having a prison is not mentioned at all, is it? You can read through it, but the word "prison" isn't mentioned.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not mentioned in this excerpt here, the word prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm dealing with the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I see Mr. Whiting shaking his head if there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would just object that that's misstates the evidence and draw the attention to page 74 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No -- well, Mr. Whiting may have missed the point. It may appear elsewhere but in relating the conversation with Celiku, according to this on page 76 and 77 in fact nothing is suggested that a prison was mentioned, and you can trawl 76 and 77 in the English version there's no reference to prison in this conversation, whatever else may be on other pages on other occasions. And I think the witness agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you on this matter of the conversation whether a further mistake has been made by you in that you did not have a conversation with Fatmir Limaj about a tractor leaving Lapusnik. Now, do you think you may have made a mistake about that as well?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain this issue yesterday. I have talked not only with Fatmir but also with many others about tractors that I have allowed to go in the direction of the villages under Serb-forces control. I thought I was wrong in doing that, letting the tractor go in that direction. And I felt I would be responsible if something occurred to them on -- along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I follow what you're saying. The question is: Do you think you may have made a mistake when one of the people you speak to was Fatmir? Because I suggest he wasn't one of the people you spoke to about a tractor at this time.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that I spoke with him about a later -- at a later time when misinformation was spread about my person. My impression was that I talked with him, but I can't give you accurate time because this is a period when major events occurred and I can't tell you if I spoke specifically with him about this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the final questions that I have for you in fact are more general and concern Fatmir himself. I just want to ask you in your dealings with Fatmir Limaj during this time and a later time as a -- as a soldier in the -- during the war, is it right that Fatmir himself gave a great deal of assistance to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's a fact of life that nobody can deny. Fatmir Limaj was the man, the key person who was committed to helping the population and they're all grateful to his military and political commitment, especially those people, that is over 70.000 persons whom Fatmir Limaj with his commitment made possible to survive in those hard times following the offensive by the Serb forces. This is my conviction regarding Fatmir Limaj, that he has helped many people and that the indictment made against him when I know that he is the person who assisted over 70.000 people, the indictment which makes those charges against him for killing civilian population makes no sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I just want specific examples, if you wouldn't mind, of the assistance he gave. I believe you may be able to describe resources that were distributed, such as food, help with education and schools, help with health centres as well. Can you describe any of those for us or not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to describe that as much as I can recollect. During that period when the population was taking shelter in passes and gorges, I remember Fatmir Limaj contributing greatly in collecting material aid, foodstuffs to distribute to the population, even the few reserves he had -- food reserves he had for his soldiers, he gave them to the civilian population. He was involved with a group of doctors to help the population. They settled in Shale valley to give aid to the population, to the injured in this gorge. And Fatmir Limaj played an extraordinary role during that time. My impressions during the speeches he gave to the civilian population to extend [as interpreted] the hardships and wait for the time when this could pass created impression that this happen man should be a member of the General Staff, and if he was not then the General Staff would probably consider him as a potential candidate at a later period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: There are no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will be asking questions last, if at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I represent Isak Musliu. I want to first of all deal with a chronology of dates, putting together everything you've been telling us over the last five days. You told us yesterday of an arrest of yourself in the year 2000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you help me, please, with the month of the year of 2000 in which you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is rather difficult for me to remember the month, but I think it must have been April of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We know that in August and in September of the year of 2001 and also in October of that year you, with the assistance of Mr. Barney Kelly, made a long witness statement to be used in the case against Milosevic. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Moving into the next year, it was in June 2002 that you sat perhaps in the very same chair you're sitting in now and gave evidence in the case against Mr. Milosevic, I think on the 5th and 6th of June. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the dates, but I remember that it was in June 2002 that I was in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In April of the following year, 2003, you gave the taped interview to among others, Mr. Lehtinen; Mr. Whiting, who's here; Mr. Cayley who isn't, that we have been seeing and reading so such about in the last few days of your evidence. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And finally in terms of this chronology a matter that you were just telling Mr. Mansfield about earlier on this afternoon, an arrest of yourself again now in March of 2004. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if I could deal, please, first of all with a little bit of background regarding yourself. It's first of all right to say, is it not, Mr. Buja, that distantly and through a cousin of yours you are related to Isak Musliu, are you not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, if you're related to his brother, there's a fair chance you might be related to him. Do you agree? Very distantly, Mr. Buja. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is that I am a cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cousin of mine is a cousin to Isak Musliu. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's right. You're in your late 30s, is that right, Mr. Buja, today?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have turned 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In 1989 you were involved in demonstrations in Kosovo regarding the political situation, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved and indeed I was one of the persons who staged them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were arrested on the 7th of June of 1989, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were interrogated for three months, often violently, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for three months on end. Violence, unprecedented violence, was used against my person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were eventually to receive a 13-year jail sentence, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The Prosecutor of your case at that hearing was somebody by the name of Denica Marinkovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That was the same woman judge who came to Racak to conduct the investigation into the massacre there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your trial for this political offence for which you were sentenced to 13 years lasted about three hours, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were regularly maltreated while serving your prison sentence, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was maltreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You served five years of that 13-year sentence, being released in 1994. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The following year, 1995, you left Kosovo to seek political asylum in Switzerland. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You became there involved in activities, rallies, and so on, mainly in Switzerland. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You first became aware, did you not, of the KLA in 1996?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware even before, but I didn't know the persons involved in the ranks of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: After the events in Prekaz in particular and the death of Adem Jashari and members of his family, if I recollect correctly, on the 5th of March 1998, you and approximately 30 other people returned or began a journey to return to your homeland to fight. Is that right, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you for that regarding background. I want to move on, please, if I may to one or two questions following on those that Mr. Mansfield along the line here asked you this afternoon regarding structure -- structure of the KLA in general terms, and then I'm going to get specific. But I want your help generally first of all. Mr. Mansfield took you to parts of your Milosevic witness statement that dealt with creation of the zones, and I'm not going to repeat it. What I'm going to do, though, is to add. Mr. Buja, in that statement which I have in front of me, and I think you do, too, in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And you're going to have to forgive me because I haven't done the reconciliation between English paging and Albanian. In the English it's page 4 of the 27 pages. And what I'm looking at, Mr. Buja, is a list of the seven zones and their areas of responsibility that you put in this statement. Have you got that? I'm not going to go into villages and the like, just the titles, as it were, of the zones, just so we can have it from you. Follow me -- will you follow me, please. The seven zones are: Drenica, Pastrik, Dukagjin, Shala, Llap, Nerodime, and Karadak. Is that right, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Would I be right in suggesting that these zones came about partly because of the response of the international community to the political plan that initially was based on the idea of liberating all Albanian territories? Is that, Mr. Buja, how the idea of these zones came about in the first place?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea for the organisation into zones was born after the political discussions and the political changes that the General Staff made by directing the war only in the territory of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: There was, was there not, a negative reaction in the international community to the idea that any war waged by the KLA would be one leading to the liberating of all Albanian territories. That was recognised, and that was why the plan changed, wasn't it, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan was changed because during the political discussions it was said that the integrity of Balkan state was being put at risk and it was surreal to wage a war in all occupied territories of Albania, and that's why the General Staff changed its policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move from what is surreal to what was, I suggest, very real, and that's the structure. I want to deal now with structure specifically, Mr. Buja, and I want to deal with a particular time period. I want to deal with the period that begins in March with the killing of Adem Jashari and his family and ends with the offensive in July. Do you understand me? That's the period I want to deal with.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: What I'm going to try and do, Mr. Buja, in a number of questions, short questions to you, is to try and put together everything you've been telling us and perhaps trying to tell us since you've been sitting in that chair. The campaign that the KLA waged in that period, March to July, was a guerrilla campaign, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be called guerrilla campaign, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It very much involved the technique, may I suggest the well-known guerrilla technique, of hit-and-run, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning in the month of March, this is how it was, such activity; but in the later period we began to apply -- we began to position these guerrilla units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Precisely. And that is how it came to be as March turned into April, for example, that small, volunteer groups formed into units or points. That's right, isn't it, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I of course speak of the form that I applied. I organised the units in Shtime and Lipjan. I explained that where the terrain was for each person to organise his unit, the horizontal layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Please listen to my questions which I'm trying to fashion Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. precisely and briefly. These units or points were small, volunteer groups, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were small, voluntary groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: They were in isolation from each other or in cooperation only by mutual agreement, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was in May and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm glad you agree with that because that's a view that this Court has expressed on a previous occasion. After the July offensive, after the offensive in late July, which was in Serb terms very successful, the KLA concentrated very much, didn't it, in the Drenica region for the most part. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mainly in Drenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: There was developing now I suggest, Mr. Buja, within the ranks of those who we could describe as members of the General Staff, what I suggest amounted to a major tactical change. And the major tactical change I suggest was about to come into operation was that the KLA would fight a more conventional military campaign. You've used the expression a "frontal war," to distinguish it from the guerrilla campaign. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct for that period when we began a different organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And consequently in the light of that decision, a new structure was required to be put in place than the one that existed before. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And so it was, Mr. Buja, I suggest, that the General Staff now decided to form things called brigades and battalions working out of the subzones that had already been created. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subzone commanders were appointed and as for the structure it was -- it came later, the one that comprised battalions, brigades, and other formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And what happened with regard to those brigades and battalions was that they did not, did they, adopt army rankings such as a brigadier in charge of a brigade, but what was created was a commander and a deputy commander and everyone else was on the same sort of level. Do you agree with that, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a level of brigade, for example, if a brigade commander was commanded -- was appointed, the commander of the other brigade would be of the same level. It took quite some time for the commands of the brigades and their structure to consolidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And as the summer turns into the autumn of 1998, there came about, Mr. Buja, I suggest, a further opportunity to consolidate and confirm this new structure. And the opportunity, I suggest, that came about is something that I don't think we've heard of yet in this trial. There was a cease-fire, wasn't there, agreed between Holbrooke and Milosevic in October of 1998. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And this cease-fire was taken, was it not, as a further opportunity by the KLA to, as I've put it, consolidate and confirm this new and very different structure to the one that had existed before the summer offensive. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's move on and deal with another topic all together, please. During the course of your interview with the ICTY in April 2003, you were asked a number of questions regarding the stopping and detaining and arresting of people who might have been thought to be collaborators. You remember a large number of questions being asked on that subject, Mr. Buja, I have no doubt?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, the interpreters can't hear you. You will understand -- it must be a tiring exercise to be in a witness box for five and a half days. Can I ask you to sit closer to the microphone and if you wouldn't mind keeping your voice up slightly. I'm going to try and be not too much longer with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I don't think I'm going to need to take you to it, but do you remember in this April 2003 interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: For Your Honours' records it's at page 61 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: -- you were talking about people who might have been taking personal revenge, settling scores for personal motives. Do you remember -- do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry. Could I just interrupt. Could there be a redaction at page 43, line 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Did I mention a name? My fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: My fault. Can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, at another part of this interview - and again I don't take you to it, you've been shown it - you talk a bit about people having guns and areas being out of the control of the KLA. Do you remember -- do you remember talking about that in the interview as well?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to see again if I could -- an attempt to summarise this aspect of it, Mr. Buja. Would you agree with this as a possibility, that there were a number of rogue elements even within the KLA who may have been settling scores for personal motives? Do you agree that's possible?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I agree with this possibility, because we could not control everything in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Another expression that you used - I wanted to ask you a little bit more about it - when answering questions yesterday you talked about the fighting of a special war against you and your comrades. Page 40 of the transcript for day 47, the 9th of March, at line 12. "During July," said you yesterday, "a special war was waged against the KLA and this war incorporated these rumours as well as different acts perpetrated by the KLA members, that people were being taken, people were being arrested." A special war waged by whom, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This special war was waged by certain mechanisms of the Serb occupying forces. And several KLA soldiers became their victim by transmitting the rumours that were going around at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to move on now to Lapusnik and various questions surrounding that place. Mr. Buja, I could take you to several different references in the transcript of the evidence you've been giving us over the last few days, but yet again in the interests of time-saving may I try to attempt a summary to see if you agree. There were, weren't there - and I'm dealing now with a period of May and June and July - in Lapusnik several units of the KLA, Celiku 3, Guri 3, and Pellumbi, and so on. There were several of them, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned this. In Lapusnik, as I had heard, there were several KLA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It would be - to borrow Mr. Mansfield's word - nonsense to suggest that there was just one commander in Lapusnik, wouldn't it? There were several commanders of -- a commander at least for each of the units, wasn't there, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the organisation at that time, each unit had its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And in the unit that I or I should say my client is most directly concerned with, Celiku 3, there were two commanders, weren't there, Voglushi and Qerqizi. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know who was the commander. I knew that Voglushi, at least he appeared to me to be a commander of a unit. And I was in good terms with him because of the assistance he provided me during fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And he also provided you assistance with regards to another matter - and I'm not going to mention the name and I would ask you not to as well - when you went to see him to do some business regarding a man who had disappeared. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke with Voglushi regarding this issue and I visited Voglushi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You told us that you went to Lapusnik and were taken by soldiers to a house where Voglushi appeared to be based. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
