utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: When I referred to the word "business" it was of course your word, not mine, but the business you had with Voglushi that day was in relation to this particular person who you'd been sent to find out what had happened to by his father, who you knew. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest a correction to some evidence you gave yesterday about this meeting, Mr. Buja. You suggested that Qerqizi was there -- in fact, you more than suggested it. You said you thought he was. I want to make it clear to you, Mr. Buja, his case is very clearly that he was not present at any meeting or discussion that you may have had with Voglushi when the subject of this person was discussed. Now, do I make myself clear to you? I am suggesting you are wrong, mistaken, in telling us that he was there. Do you accept what I put to you or do you insist that he was there? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot insist because I knew Qerqiz very little at that time; I knew his brother better. I said that he could have been there and that I could have seen him in Lapusnik region even in that instance, although there were many soldiers in that region and it was difficult to tell who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: A good deal of the passage in the interview that deals with this meeting seeks to try and show or deal with where this meeting with Voglushi took place. Do you recollect it happening in a private house belonging to a villager, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a village house. It belonged to a villager.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence correctly to indicate that you did not spend a very great deal of time in Lapusnik that day, at least you didn't spend the night there. Your meeting took place, you dealt with events, you met the person concerned, and you left. Now, have I understood your evidence correctly or did you spend the night in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not spend the night there, and yesterday I said that I'm not familiar with Lapusnik village. I am familiar with Lapusnik as a region. Even today I do not know the house that I visited and where I stayed for an hour or two, but surely I did not spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Before that visit to Voglushi for that purpose, had you ever been to the village of Lapusnik before?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I hadn't been there before. Now I don't remember whether it was before that or after that I went to a territory that was also called Lapusnik region where I collected some KLA emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I have no doubt, Mr. Buja, that you may recollect during the course of your April 2003 interview you were asked a number of questions regarding whether there might have been a prison in Lapusnik. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you remember what your answers were to the questions as to whether there was a prison in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately I can remember what I said regarding the prison or the camp that was alleged to have existed in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And approximately what did you say do you recollect?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately what I said was that I was not able to know about this issue and that there couldn't be a prison because as Kosova Liberation Army we didn't have investigation bodies or judicial bodies and this did not make sense to me. But I said that every unit could have had a stopping point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And by "stopping point," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "stopping point" we understood a place where soldiers were positioned on a road used by civilian population where people were being stopped and identification was produced by them in order to find out the reason and the purpose of their visit to that particular location. This was the way we stopped people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If I were to use the word "checkpoint" to describe such a place, would you agree with that word?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a sort of a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, what we know in relation - and again I'm not going to use the name - in relation to the gentleman about whom you spoke to Voglushi, it seems, does it not, from what you tell us, Mr. Buja, that in his case at least it went a little further than just being stopped on the road. He was taken somewhere to be questioned. Is that your understanding of the position with regard to this gentleman? Please remember not to mention his name.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that that person, at least this is what Voglushi told me, this person was stopped because of driving fast, and when the KLA soldiers wanted to stop him he didn't do so. Therefore, he was forced to stop at gun point. After his vehicle was checked, certain addresses were found in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, you've told us all of that already at some length and in some detail; regrettably, it's not an answer to the question I asked you which is: Did you understand therefore, that once all of that had happened he, this man, was taken somewhere while inquiries of some sort or made concerning him? Is that what you understood?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot call it inquiry, but this person, his identity was verified, checked. That's why he was stopped because he committed a violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Two questions arising, Mr. Buja. First of all, did Voglushi tell you on what road this man was travelling when he was stopped? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him telling me which road it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Secondly, did Voglushi or anyone else tell you where he was kept in Lapusnik while these inquiries were being made? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did Voglushi or anyone else tell you or show you a place where people were being held in circumstances such as these? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In circumstances such as those, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did Voglushi or anyone else tell you or show you a place where people were being held in any other circumstances, yes or no, in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We might have made some jokes, but no he didn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you shown any photographs during your interview, not of people but of places, in April 2003, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let's see if I can bring that moment back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P6 with the assistance of the usher, the locations booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we have a copy of it over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting -- oh, we've got one. Thank you very much. Do Your Honours have this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: As if we're not as familiar with it as we can be. I'm grateful. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, would you open this booklet up, please, to page 1, which is an aerial photograph of a place called the Lapusnik farm compound. We all recognise that looking at aerial photographs is difficult; I'm going to get you on the ground in a minute. But first of all, have you seen this aerial photograph before?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to recognise it because the village houses resemble one another like an egg to another egg.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could you go please to photograph number 4 -- rather, paragraph number 14 to start with, sorry Mr. Buja. Keep your finger in 4 but go to 14. Keep your finger in 4, hold on to it, and go to photograph 14, please, 1-4. 14 is a photograph showing the entrance gate of this compound, and over the page at 15 shows a clearer photograph of the same gate, Mr. Buja. Just look at it, if you would, please. Now go back to where perhaps you've kept your finger and you will see a building which is the rest of the building you see partly in photograph 14 and 15. I'm going to do this all of a piece for you to you can help us if possible. Can you also look at photograph 11. And it's showing you the outsides of buildings, and 7 and 6 and 5. Mr. Buja, have you ever seen any of those photographs before, and specifically have you seen them during the course of your interview in April 2003?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They don't look like the same photographs that I've seen. It is possible that photograph bearing number 15 was shown to me. I'm not quite sure, but it is possible. And here I said that the buildings were of the post-war period and that I could not identify that place as one that I've been to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, the photographs I have shown you were not, I repeat not, photographs of the place where you met with Voglushi. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot be precise whether these are the photographs because I stayed in this village very briefly and I did not know this village. I said that it was a one-storey house and as any other village house it had a well and a storage place. It was just a simple village house and I cannot identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The difference between it and the photographs of the place you've just been looking at, Mr. Buja, I suggest, is that the house you met Voglushi in was not in a compound, was it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that these are the houses because the houses here are two-storey ones except for one on one of the photographs which is a one-storey house. To my recollection the house where I met Voglushi was a one-story house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you understand the word "compound"? Do you understand what that means?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't mean to be rude. We have to be precise here. There are, I promise you, important reasons for these questions, so please forgive me. The house in which you met Voglushi was not in a compound, was it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what I've seen, it was not a complex of houses, it was a village of house [as interpreted] which I observed as such. It had some --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, did you want to continue?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- other features around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, the translation. Thank you. Mr. Buja, once -- different topic. We've left Lapusnik. Once you became a commander in the way that you have described, Mr. Buja, did there come a time - and I suggest there did and I suggest it was after the creation of the battalions and the brigades - when the military police were formed? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The structuring of the military police in my zone came quite late. It was in December or January 1998/1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And it's important to recognise, is it not, Mr. Buja, that the introduction of the military police occurred at different stages in different zones. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In due course, these military policemen and indeed women were to be given, to mark them out, a different kind of uniform. Is that right, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: A black uniform with a PU on an armband or on a cap badge. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Their role, their function, was to not only keep order within the ranks of the KLA, but also to assist as best they could with keeping some sort of law and order and help to the civilian population. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were mainly the tasks of the military police to check the behaviour of KLA soldiers and, when necessary, to assist the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, you know a lot about this, don't now, Mr. Buja? The military police, I mean.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the military police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were Qerqizi's boss when he became a military police officer in late 1998, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Isak Musliu, Qerqizi, became commander of the military police company in his zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And you were the person, were you not, who explained some of his responsibilities to him when, for example, he was appointed temporary chief of a branch of the military police known as ZKZ in the Nerodime zone. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: ZKZ and the military police are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, they are. ZKZ is a counter-intelligence unit within the military police, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way our organisation was was different. This was a special unit or sector, this ZKZ. In the context of the police, there was also a similar sector but at a lower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree that in February 1999 in fact, is it within your knowledge that Isak Musliu, Qerqizi, was appointed temporary chief of ZKZ? Is that within your knowledge, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Qerqizi was appointed commander of the military police in my zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He was well thought of and very highly regarded as a law-keeper, wasn't he, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I became acquainted with his activity, he was a very law-abiding person, a very distinguished soldier, and he did a very good job in restructuring the police -- in structuring the police with whom he worked. He was a very disciplined soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I just want to deal, finally, with a particular moment regarding the war and regarding a meeting you had with Qerqiz. But before I get to that, Mr. Buja, do you agree that on the occasions - and there were several - during the period up to the Serb offensive in July you would meet Qerqiz from time to time usually in Kroimire. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Qerqiz, whose name I recalled later as such, because -- I couldn't know him because I left Kosova at a very early age, at 22, and I returned at 28. But I did see Qerqiz in Kroimire, but especially so in -- I saw his ability. On -- especially during the war on the 24th of July, when together we entered Fushtice village to recapture the positions of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, you and I must be linking on a telepathic level, Mr. Buja, because that's exactly what I was going to put to you. On the 24th of July you met Qerqizi - and I can be very specific about this - at about lunchtime and you were with Ramiz Qeriqi, Luani, and this was just before entering Fustica. And there you were with Luani and Qerqizi, who had just come from Rahovec met you there. Now, do you remember this meeting, Mr. Buja? You plainly do. Do you remember the detail now as I put it to you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to recall the details, which I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: All right. What I'm going to do in the interests of time saving, and I can do it quickly, is may I just put to you, sir, please one or two matters and see if you agree if this rings any bells. He met you and Luani. It was a dangerous spot you were in. You were in severe danger of being shelled. Fustica and Sankovc were burning. Qerqizi decided to attack the Serb forces in Fustica and took up into his hand for that purpose a 60-millimetre hand-held rocket-propelled grenade launcher and he advised on how to focus the attack. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Most of the soldiers in Fushtice and in that checkpoint that was between Fushtice and Shale were in a difficult situation. They didn't have trenches and bunkers and they were exposed to danger. It's true that that Qerqiz came to us and suggested an operation to carry out in Fushtice village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And I suggest, typical of him, he learned there were three or four soldiers, KLA soldiers, trapped in positions in Fustica and he decided with his RPG to take two or three men to try and save them. You said that you were going to Blinaje because Blinaje was under attack as well. Do you remember this happening, Mr. Buja?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with Qerqiz and some other soldiers we set out to enter the village I mentioned earlier, Fushtice, and at the time that we were engaged in that area of operation we heard shots in Blinaje. And I told Qerqiz that we have to pull back to go and take part in Blinaje fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's all I ask you. Thank you for your patience. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, if you could open up the transcript, please, from the OTP interview and turn, please, to page 81, and it's page 68 of the English transcript. And, Mr. Buja, once you get to page 81 I'd draw your attention to the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could switch to the Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "A.C.: Lapusnik, the place where the prisoners were held, you say that there were also KLA soldiers based at the same location? "S.B.: As far as what I've seen, yes. "A.C.: Now, you mentioned earlier to us that one of the subunits within Lapusnik was called the Celiku unit. And that Celiku unit was based at the location that we've just been speaking about, wasn't it? "S.B.: Yeah, Celiku 3 was as I said stationed on this side of the road, Klecka side. On the other side where this Guri 3 point was I was supposed to have a special permission to go there or support them there because I could have been arrested myself as well. "O.L.: But I think what Mr. Cayley tried to ask you was the main -- we call it headquarters, you might call it point, but was the main point for Celiku 3 this point? "S.B.: I can talk about things that I've seen for myself. I cannot say there was the command place, let's say. So I've seen people like Voglushi and Qerqizi there. Because I don't know -- I don't know. I'm not sure about whether it's safe to say it was the command place there or not. "O.L.: No, no, but did you get the impression that that was the command place for Celiku 3? "S.B.: Yes, because -- yes, because I asked to be taken to this Celiku 3 headquarters or point, whatever you -- "A.C.: And this is the same place where the prisoners were held? "S.B.: Yes, Celiku 3. "O.L.: Okay. The times you visited this -- the camp, let's call it a camp or the main -- this place in Lapusnik, were these all occasions during this so-called first -- first offensive during July 1998? "S.B.: Yeah, I was -- I am talking about June, because in July even if I was willing or needed to go there, I couldn't go there."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, do you remember now that when you went to get that person released - and again please do not use his name - to get that person released from Lapusnik that you went to Celiku 3?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I remember that I asked for Voglushi, and I didn't know which unit was stationed there. I have always talked about on the basis of the impressions I created about the way -- or the organisation was. I have described something which I didn't know for sure because the Celiku unit number 3, the Pellumbi unit, and other unit as far as I was concerned might have been stationed on one side of the road or on the other side. I didn't know, so I didn't speak with full authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you agree that when you went to try to get this person released, you asked to be taken to Celiku 3, you went to Celiku 3. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked to be taken to Voglushi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the place where the prisoners were held in Lapusnik was at Celiku 3. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - and I think I have explained -- clarified this issue with you - I cannot talk about a prison or a camp because in my view it was not a -- such a place. As far as I knew, every unit had what we said a checking point, but this interpretation as a camp or a prison camp, it was not said by me. It was put to me by the others, those who asked me questions. So I don't know about a place where detainees were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going -- I think I'll be about ten or 15 minutes longer. I don't know if this is where we should break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is, and we'll resume at 10 minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, in August and September did Ramiz Qeriqi, Luan, stay in Kroimire?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August and September of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, of 1998.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 198 -- in 1998, in August and September, as far as I remember he was there even though at the time of August I went to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecution Exhibit 155, please. And that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, are you aware that on this date, on the 16th of August, 1998, Ramiz Qeriqi was appointed to be the commander of the Ruzhdi Selihu Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may express my view about this. Even though I didn't take part in this structure of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question is: Are you aware that he was appointed to be the commander of the Ruzhdi Selihu battalion even though you were in a different structure?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war I heard that he was commander of Ruzhdi Selihu Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was within the 121st Brigade, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Battalion Ruzhdi Selihu was part of Brigade 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the 121 Brigade was within the Pastrik subzone, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Initially it became -- from subzone it became Pastrik zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so Kroimire was within the Pastrik subzone, was it not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the offensive it came within the Pastrik operational subzone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact the municipality of Lipjan was divided between Nerodimlje and Pastrik, some villages in Lipjan were in the Pastrik subzone and some were in the Nerodimlje subzone. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say "after the offensive," you're talking about after the offensive of July 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the end of the offensive was end of July and beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecution Exhibit 159, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Those villages were within the 121 Brigade as it was formed after the first offensive, isn't that right, the villages that appear on Prosecution Exhibit 159?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, the villages of Kroimire, Pjetershtice, Fushtice, up to Magura came within the zone covered by Brigade 121 after the offensive, that is August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the division between the subzone of Drenica and the subzone of Pastrik --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That document can be taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The division between the subzone of Drenica and the subzone of Pastrik was at the Peja-Pristina highway, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were a segment of this highway. There were also a range of mountains which divided these two subzones. I cannot tell you for sure the exact territory falling within each subzone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could with the assistance of the usher put before the witness a letter dated 1 April 2004, and have copies provided to the Court and to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, the letter is in English, of course, so I will read it so it can be translated into your language. It's from the Office of the Prosecutor, Carla del Ponte, the Prosecutor, to the commander of KFOR, General Kammerhoff dated 1 April 2004. "Dear General Kammerhoff, "I understand from my field office in Pristina that Mr. Shukri Buja is being detained on your order pursuant to authority granted to you by U.N. Security Council Resolution 1244. "Whilst I can make no comment regarding the current allegations against Mr. Buja, I can inform you of the following information which I think may be helpful to you in the current situation. "I am quite certain that you or members of your staff will have information concerning Mr. Buja's involvement in events in Kosovo after 1998. However, you should also know that he has cooperated with investigations conducted in Kosovo by my office. This has been in respect of inquiries against both Serb and Kosovar Albanian perpetrators. "You should also know that Mr. Buja testified about Slobodan Milosevic on 5 and 6 June, 2002, and that he has agreed to testify in a forthcoming case which concerns Kosovar Albanian perpetrators. I can confirm that during recent interviews conducted with Mr. Buja by members of my office he was reasonable and personable. I understand he has made the same impression on members of KFOR. "I trust the above may be of some assistance to you." Mr. Buja, do you remember that being the letter that was read to you were -- when a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor came to met with you while you were being detained in March and April of 2004?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be given a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P161, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, sir, I want to ask you about a follow-up on a question that you were asked by Mr. Topolski. He asked you if the organisation into subzones was the result of a negative reaction in the international community to the idea that any war waged by the KLA would be one leading to the liberating of all Albanian territories. And your response was: "The plan was changed because during the political discussions it was said that the integrity of Balkan states was -- a Balkan state was being put at risk and it was surreal to wage a war in all occupied territories of Albania, and that's why the General Staff changed its policy." My question is: Are you talking about July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period when negotiations started. It was August, September, October, because the change from subzones into zones, for this the decision was made sometime in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you testified that you were appointed to be the commander of the subzone of Nerodimlje on the 6th of July, 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was -- became the commander of the subzone on the 6th of July, but the decision to transform the subzones into zones was taken later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that taken, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in November. It was issued to all the subzones to start restructuring into zones and no longer as subzones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall an interview that Jakup Krasniqi gave in the beginning of July to a German newspaper in which he called for the liberation of all Albanian lands that led to some controversy?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read that interview but I heard about the debates it led to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And those debates centred on the very issue you've talked about, whether the aim of the Kosovo Liberation Army should be a broad one of liberating and uniting all Albanian territories, or whether it should be focused on the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that initially the aim of the KLA was to liberate the territories, Albanian territories, which were occupied. But later the aim changed and everything was done in the territory of Kosova. And the change, the military change in the organisation occurred later. From subzones, the decision was made to refer to them as zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did the aim change of the KLA? When was that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the talks held in August, September, and October. The decision was made in November as far as I remember on changing the military structure as well. So the political change must have occurred earlier than the military one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Understood. My question just is: If the military occurred in November, do you know when the political change occurred?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the time for the political change because at that time I was not in Kosova, so I followed events from outside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall if that political change resulted in a change in the oath that was -- that soldiers would give to -- when they joined the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if the oath was changed, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember that -- if the oath at one time contained language about liberating the Albanian territories and that that language was later taken out of the oath? Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the oath I myself gave for the liberation of Albanian-occupied territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you give that oath?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave that before I joined the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember what month?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the month, but I do remember that I took such an oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But when you say before you joined the war, is that before March 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before March even though the form of the oath was not the same as it became later, when I read the oath before the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Later did the oath -- later was that part of the oath deleted --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt, but in my respectful submission we're about 5.000 miles away from my cross-examination of this witness on the creation of zones and whether there was born of an aborted political decision, and now into oath-taking which I don't think anyone cross-examined at all. I wonder if the witness who is in his sixth day of evidence, whether this is of any assistance to the Court at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The connecting link that I see is whether the oath related to zones or not, which was your question. Now, I'm about to turn to Mr. Whiting to see whether he really has a point there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I made no linkage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You didn't, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: What's being developed is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But the response may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know. That's what I'm about to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was an apparent linkage in my mind. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First of all, this was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That doesn't get it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I understand, I understand, but Mr. Topolski made a reference to this being the sixth day of evidence. But the linkage is -- Mr. Topolski made a linkage between the creation of subzones to the change in the political strategy of the KLA, and I'm just -- it's a simple follow-up question about whether this -- and trying to locate the timing of this change and whether it was reflected in the oath that was given, and that's -- simply it's a follow-on of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the point of the oath?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That could be significant in other -- in other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But how is it re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's a follow-on from an issue that was touched on in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It might have brought it to your mind, but I don't see that it's connected in a way that justifies re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, if that's the Court's view, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was my last question. It's a shame to lose it, but that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, that concludes the questions that are asked of you so that you are now free to leave and return to your home. The officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Mansfield, you get out of my arc of vision. It's a good thing I've got spotters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'll try and get a flag or an oath maybe. The -- I didn't want to delay this witness, recognising how long he's been here, but I wonder if he might be asked to remain just for a few minutes longer or not leave the building. The reason goes back to a matter I raised earlier. It didn't develop at that point because of the need, in a sense, to ensure the end of his evidence, at least today if at all possible, and that relates to the notes that were taken he says by the investigator at the proofing. I've mentioned this to Mr. Whiting; he's not prepared to allow us to see these notes. In my submission, in the particular circumstances, which as we're in public session I won't develop them but Your Honour is well aware of what the particular circumstances are that relate to this witness, it is imperative that we do see these notes because of the issues that still remain to be determined particularly by Your Honour in relation to the status of either what he said before in the April 2003 interview or in relation to his current testimony or plainly, finally, a mixture of both. Now factors that will bear upon how that is assessed may well arise out of the notes, remembering of course that he says he did not have - and I think it's agreed that he didn't have a written transcript in Albanian of what he said in 2003, albeit he had some CDs to which he says he was unable to access. So it's in that context that he comes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you a moment. If you would please ensure Mr. Buja doesn't leave the witness unit for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. Therefore, the -- it's in that context that he hasn't got an actual record in front of him, or he hasn't had, as to how it is that -- and what it is that he says about his recollection of not only what he said in the 2003 interview but of course his memory of what it was he was describing that dates further back, namely structure. Now, the supplemental information sheet that we were given I read out before. It is short in the extreme and ambiguous. It merely says: "The witness has indicated that the structure," it doesn't say which structure, it doesn't say at particularly what point other than throughout May and July. One assumes he's obviously talking about the KLA, but it doesn't say that, "in his OTP interview of April of 2003 is not what existed." Well, it must be some other questions were asked. So was he asked what did exist? And was he asked a little bit more about what he thought he had said in the April 2003 interview about structure that differed from what he was wanting to say about the structure? It may mean that different words were used, it may mean that he used those words but he meant something else; I don't know what it is. And of course the same goes for the second sentence: "He says now that Fatmir Limaj was not his commander." Well, had he thought that he had said that Fatmir Limaj was his commander? Or that he'd said that but he didn't mean it? Or what? We submit this is most unsatisfactory in relation to this witness, and you will recall we haven't made this application every time a witness comes. But in relation to this one we say it's significant. And as a matter of, we say, some authority, it is clear in other cases going on in this building at the moment that -- and of course they're not binding upon Your Honours, but it is a practice that's plainly adopted by the Office of the Prosecutor in other cases where the notes are handed over almost as a matter of course. And the case to which I refer is Oric, Naser Oric. We have the transcript in which this very issue isn't argued; it's merely the Learned Tribunal asking the Prosecutor for the notes because everyone else has got them except themselves. They're handed over, not a problem. There cannot be any conceivable reason why the notes in this case cannot be made available from the investigator. When it suits the Prosecution, we get the notes, for example, in this instance. We've got the investigator's notes when there's an allegation that obviously the Prosecution do not wish to accept concerning his being told not to see the Defence; then we get the notes. There can't be anything sensitive in these notes, it's not suggested there are. At the moment, it's merely you can't have them. And there's no reason as to why we can't have them, other than the Prosecutor saying in his view they're not relevant. Well, I think that's perhaps the understatement of the century because when one has statements made by a witness in this case about relevant matters in the case, the idea that we can't see the underlying documentation in relation to relevant statements is, we say, not in the interests of justice and certainly not in the interests of a final assessment of how Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this witness came to, as it were, make changes and the nature of the changes. So I merely ask at this stage that Your Honour request the Prosecution to allow us to see these notes, and the reason I've asked the witness to remain and you have kindly asked that he does is that he should be shown these notes to see whether in fact he agrees that that was what was said. Because once again, this is a witness who, we would submit, has been treated so far by the Prosecution quite appallingly by not being given, despite requests, the written transcript that he undoubtedly required. And most witnesses, we submit, have as a matter of right a copy if they wish is of what they have said, whoever they are. So once again he's not shown these proofing notes but he has a recollection of some "issues being raised by the Prosecution." Well, what issues? How were they raised? What were the framework of the questions, and so forth? If they're lasting an hour, there's a lot being said than we've got in these two short sentences. So please may we have the notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just formally support that and simply add this, that if it is the case as Mr. Mansfield has just indicated that it is Mr. Whiting saying in our view they are not relevant, then the entire jurisprudence that in my jurisdiction fundamentally altered the rules and regulations governed disclosure were born of such a high-handed attitude, whereby the Prosecution decides in its own course what is and what is not relevant. Your Honour, I simply add that in general and specific support of my learned friend's application.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think because of the entire nature of the statements is of critical importance to the Trial Chamber, specifically with regard to this witness, it is a specious assertion to say that notes concerning any of those discussions are not relevant. I would support the application made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me first address "appalling," then I'll go to "high-handed," and then to "specious." With respect to whether the Prosecution has treated this witness in an appalling manner, I think there's no dispute that the Prosecution within days of being asked by the witness to give the transcript, provided five CDs with the witness's transcripts of all his interviews and testimony and statements. The witness himself said that he never went back -- came back to the OTP to say that he was unable to open up those CDs. So as far as the Prosecution was aware, the witness had been provided those statements. With respect to whether we are high-handed as a Prosecution in deciding matters of disclosure, I would submit that in this jurisdiction and certainly in many others, it is the Prosecution's responsibility to make decisions about what needs to be disclosed, whether it's Rule 68 or Rule 66(B). Coming to the specific issue at hand, and that is proofing, this very issue has been litigated in this courtroom and this Court has endorsed the practice that has been followed in this case and with all the other witnesses that it is -- that the Prosecution will disclose -- will -- and will decide what to disclose important matters, whether they be Rule 68 or Rule 66(B) new evidence that should be brought to the attention of the Defence. That was done in this case. Now the question is: Should there be a departure from that rule because of the particular circumstances of this witness. And try as I might, despite the overblown language, I cannot discern a reason why there should be a departure from the rule in this case. This -- for one thing, I think this issue should have been raised earlier, on cross-examination. If what Mr. Mansfield is imagining is bringing back the witness to re-open cross-examination, then this should have been done when he was cross-examining the witness and he raised the issue for the first time. And when he did he suggested he would come back to it, I thought he would come back to it before he finished his cross-examination and there was re-direct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you need pursue that point further. In view of Mr. Mansfield's indication at the time, if the matter warrants the notes being provided, that issue won't alter the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Understood. In any event, I don't -- this issue has been already, I would submit, well mined and explored with the witness. The Prosecution, as I said, has made its disclosure about important matters that occurred at the -- at the proofing. Those -- those are the important matters that arose. Those have been disclosed. I don't see -- I simply cannot understand how it could benefit the Chamber any further to have these notes disclosed and have further questions -- further rounds of questioning about these notes when the important matters, I would submit, have already been disclosed and the issue has already been thoroughly discussed with the witness about what his impressions were and what he thought happened at the proofing, which is really ultimately the matter, if the Court is assessing credibility. So I don't think there's anything here that warrants a departure from the rule that's been laid down by the Court, and it's for that reason that the Prosecution -- and not for any high-handedness. But it is for that reason that the Prosecution has resisted turning over its notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, has the relevance of those notes potentially to the Defence been reconsidered in light of the motion that is before the Chamber as to the potential use that might be made of the past statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Certainly. I have thought of that and it's perhaps the -- the limits of my ability to think at this late hour, but I don't see any benefit or any real connection why this would be helpful or relevant for that issue. But if that's -- certainly if it's going -- if it could be useful for that issue and there is some linkage there that I'm failing to appreciate, then perhaps that's an opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, this is a linkage that neither Defence counsel nor the Chamber can make at the present time. And that's why if there is to be reliance on the Prosecution carefully accepting and honouring its responsibilities as to disclosure of material of potential relevance to the Defence, there needs to be care in the appreciation of circumstances such as those that the notes relate to as to the precise way in which the witness came to change, if that's what occurred, the account he'd given previously to any account that he may have given in the course of the proofing. Now, it may be that no account was given in the course of the proofing; the Chamber doesn't know that, the Defence don't know that. And it needs -- just what did occur needs to be considered, I would have thought, by the Prosecution with care against the possibility that the circumstances of what occurred at that could well be of materiality to the reliability of what was said earlier or not. The real force now is that in the particular case of this witness, whom on notice from you is changing his position - and I say nothing whether it is a change of position or whether that was merely the way you understood it at the time - you are now moving that we should not only accept the previous position as evidence relevant to the facts of the case but should prefer that to what the present evidence is. Have I said enough to emphasise the importance potentially and why it is that there should be a very careful appreciation of what did occur at that interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think so. Yes, Your Honour. I would note that the Prosecution has in its disclosure indicated that there was a change between the prior interview and proofing, the proofing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There you call it disclosure. I would call it simply notice of changed evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, fair enough. Fair enough. Which is what I thought was required under the Court's ruling with regard to proofing. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Some ground has moved since that ruling was given, and I've tried to assist you to focus on that change.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. And frankly, to avoid -- I'll just concede and just show them the notes and not make them -- a mountain out of this. I was trying to stand on principle, but maybe this time practicality is more the order of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, principle you see from the previous decision of the Chamber, the way the Chamber sees the principle. My concern at the present time is that there has come to be potentially a very considerable significance to this particular proofing or interview before the evidence was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. I didn't mean to say that -- I didn't mean to suggest that it was not -- principled, what the Court was suggesting. I simply meant I was standing on the wrong principle, let's say. In any event, I'm happy to provide the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where does that then -- I don't know how long they are. Where does that leave Mr. Mansfield and other counsel and the witness with his running shoes on outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They're four pages long, Your Honour. They're extremely sketchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have one or more copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could pass them now to Mr. Mansfield and the Chamber will sit patiently and it may be possible for Defence counsel to indicate whether the witness is needed further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, my attention is being drawn to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Sorry. May I thank Your Honours on behalf of all of us for the opportunity to look at them. The short position is that we don't think there's anything in here which should detain the witness, but it does raise a large number of questions. And rather than, as it were, raise them all in public across the chamber, if we may be permitted to raise them with Mr. Whiting about these notes and I'm happy for -- if Your Honours would like to see them for them to be copied. It may be of advantage for them to be translated because the writing is difficult to follow. And may I just say at once, are there any more notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the Chamber will remain innocent of the contents of the notes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you don't need any permission from us to have discussions with Prosecuting counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And if we hear no more, we hear no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I have a feeling you might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is a little of a quarter of an hour of much value with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honour the next witness has protective measures, so a number of minutes would be required in any event to arrange the courtroom. So I think probably we should just start tomorrow with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tomorrow. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know, I was given to understand that there were some issues to be canvassed in relation to this witness before he gives evidence. They would doubtless need to be canvassed in private session. I don't know whether that will be time well spent now or saved for tomorrow or whether we feel we've had enough for the today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've certainly got 17 or 18 minutes' worth of energy left, but the business of getting the witness in leaves little time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: As I understand it was matters to be raised before the witness came into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Unless I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I just indicate that the indication to the witness unit that Mr. Buja is now at an end and the witness may go, if that could be communicated. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is indeed a very brief matter, but if we could just do it in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
